141: A is correct because Amazon CloudFront is a global CDN whose edge locations cache content close to users worldwide, and it can serve both static and dynamic content by using the ALB as a custom origin. This delivers the personalized portal output with the least latency for a global audience while keeping the application stack in a single Region. Route 53 latency or geolocation routing across two Regions only directs users to the closest ALB and does not cache content at the edge, so it cannot match CloudFront's performance. Serving dynamic content directly from the ALB would force distant users to traverse long network paths for that content.
142: C is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses that are advertised from AWS edge locations, routes user traffic to the nearest edge over the AWS global network, and forwards to a Network Load Balancer, which is the load balancer that supports UDP traffic. EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group support the modified Linux kernel and provide a highly available, scalable front-end tier. Application Load Balancers and API Gateway only handle HTTP/HTTPS, Lambda cannot run a custom kernel, and CloudFront does not support arbitrary UDP protocols.
143: D is correct because Amazon ECS packages the application's components as separate containerized services that different teams can own and deploy independently, breaking the monolith into smaller applications while reusing the existing front-end and backend code with minimal change. ECS with an ALB and Auto Scaling provides a highly scalable, managed orchestration solution with less operational overhead than managing EC2 instances directly. Refactoring to Lambda or Amplify would require significant code changes, and raw EC2 instances impose more management burden.
144: B is correct because an Aurora Replica offloads the heavy monthly reporting read workload from the writer instance, eliminating the ReadIOPS and CPUUtilization spikes on the primary while keeping the ecommerce workload performing well. Aurora Replicas use the same instance class, making this far more cost-effective than a larger instance class or additional provisioned IOPS, and the reporting workload does not justify a separate Redshift cluster. The replica is a native Aurora feature that requires no data migration or pipeline maintenance.
145: D is correct because migrating the database to Aurora MySQL removes the database from the single overloaded EC2 instance, and an AMI-based launch template with an EC2 Auto Scaling group attached to an ALB lets the application scale seamlessly in response to demand. Using a Spot Fleet in the Auto Scaling group significantly reduces compute cost while the ALB distributes traffic and maintains availability as instances scale. The other options only provide a fixed second instance or a manual type change, which does not deliver seamless scaling.
146: B is correct because Reserved Instances provide the largest discount for the steady, predictable baseline usage that runs overnight and on weekends, while Spot Instances supply the additional capacity needed during the 8-hour daily peak at steep discounts. Because the application is stateless behind an ALB, any Spot interruption during peak scaling can be tolerated by the Auto Scaling group launching replacements, preserving availability. Using Spot for the entire workload risks interruptions to the baseline, and On-Demand or Dedicated Instances cost more for predictable usage.
147: B is correct because storing the logs in Amazon S3 and applying S3 Lifecycle policies automatically transitions objects older than 1 month to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest-cost storage class, satisfying the 10-year retention at minimal cost. Lifecycle policies run natively on S3 objects with no servers or backup software to manage, so recent logs remain in S3 for fast troubleshooting access. CloudWatch Logs storage at more than 10 TB per month would be prohibitively expensive, and AWS Backup is not the mechanism for tiering S3 objects.
148: D is correct because configuring an Amazon SQS queue as the on-failure destination captures the events that the Lambda function fails to process due to network connectivity issues, so no notification is lost. The function can later process the queued messages, guaranteeing that all notifications are eventually processed without manual reruns. Increasing memory or CPU, adding Availability Zones, or adjusting the SNS retry strategy does not guarantee delivery after retries are exhausted.
149: A is correct because an Amazon SQS FIFO queue preserves the exact order in which messages are sent and received, maintaining the required ordering throughout processing, and a Lambda function processing from the queue is a fully managed, low-overhead pattern. A standard queue provides at-least-once delivery without ordering guarantees, and SNS topics do not guarantee message ordering or provide the buffering and retry semantics of a queue.
150: A is correct because Amazon CloudWatch composite alarms combine multiple metric alarms so that an alarm state only triggers when the CPU utilization alarm and the high read IOPS alarm breach simultaneously, which matches the requirement to act only when both conditions occur together. Composite alarms reduce false alarms by treating short CPU bursts alone as non-actionable, something single metric alarms with multiple thresholds cannot reliably express. Dashboards and Synthetics canaries provide visibility or endpoint monitoring but do not implement combined alarming logic.
151: A is correct because AWS Control Tower implements data residency guardrails, which are preventive controls that deny internet access and deny resource provisioning in all AWS Regions except ap-northeast-3, enforcing compliance automatically. C is correct because AWS Organizations service control policies are preventive guardrails that block VPC internet connectivity, such as attaching internet gateways, and deny actions in every Region except ap-northeast-3 across all accounts in the organization. The other options rely on detective controls or network ACLs and IAM policies that are either not preventive, not centrally enforceable, or trivially bypassed.
152: D is correct because AWS Lambda functions invoked by Amazon EventBridge scheduled rules can automatically start and stop the RDS for MySQL DB instance on the 12-hour daily schedule, so the company only pays for the database while the training application is in use. This is a fully serverless automation pattern that requires no persistent infrastructure to manage. The other options either add unnecessary EC2 instances and IAM complexity, use ElastiCache in an unsupported way, or rely on Systems Manager for a task Lambda handles natively.
153: D is correct because an S3 Lifecycle policy automatically transitions ringtone objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days, cutting storage costs for the infrequently downloaded older files while keeping recently accessed files in S3 Standard where they remain readily available. Since the files are at least 128 KB, they exceed the size threshold where Standard-IA is cost-effective, and the transition happens automatically with no retrieval of the most popular content required. Storing everything in Standard-IA from creation would raise costs for actively downloaded new ringtones, and S3 Inventory only reports on objects rather than moving them.
154: B is correct because S3 Object Lock in compliance mode applies a true WORM (write once, read many) configuration with a 365-day retention period that prevents any user, including root and administrators, from modifying or deleting objects before the retention expires, satisfying the immutable 1-year medical trial requirement. Compliance mode cannot be shortened or removed, unlike governance mode which privileged users can bypass, and IAM roles and Lambda hash tracking cannot prevent all deletion or modification by every user.
155: C is correct because Amazon CloudFront is a global CDN that caches the media files from the S3 buckets at edge locations around the world, giving users fast, reliable access regardless of geographic location, and it supports confidential content through signed URLs and origin access controls. The other services do not cache content at the edge: DataSync is a migration service, Global Accelerator optimizes TCP and UDP routing to endpoints but does not cache S3 objects, and SQS is a messaging queue.
156: A is correct because Amazon Athena is a serverless query service that runs one-time queries directly against data staged in S3 with no infrastructure to manage, and Amazon QuickSight is a managed BI service for building KPI dashboards, giving teams analytics with minimal operational overhead. E is correct because AWS Lake Formation blueprints with AWS Glue crawl the disparate database and streaming sources, extract the data, and load it into the S3 data lake in Parquet format, providing a fully managed ingestion pipeline without custom code. Custom Lambda functions, Kinesis Data Analytics, and OpenSearch clusters would all add significantly more operational burden and cost.
157: D is correct because exporting the Aurora PostgreSQL cluster's audit logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs allows the company to retain the audit logs indefinitely, since CloudWatch Logs has no mandatory retention limit. E is correct because AWS Backup can take and manage the Aurora backups and retain them for 5 years, since Aurora's native automated backup retention caps out well below 5 years and cannot be extended with a lifecycle policy. A manual snapshot is point-in-time only and cannot enforce ongoing 5-year retention by itself, and native automated backups cannot be retained that long.
158: A is correct because Amazon CloudFront is a global content delivery network that improves performance for both live real-time video streaming and on-demand playback by delivering the streams through edge locations close to the worldwide audience, with high sustained throughput for video workloads. CloudFront natively supports both live streaming and on-demand video use cases. Global Accelerator and Route 53 optimize routing but do not cache or deliver streaming media content, and S3 Transfer Acceleration only speeds uploads to S3.
159: A is correct because creating an API Gateway usage plan with an API key shared only with genuine users allows the company to throttle and meter legitimate traffic and block requests that do not present a valid key, mitigating the fraudulent botnet traffic. C is correct because AWS WAF can be integrated with API Gateway to target malicious request patterns and known bad IP addresses from botnets and filter them out before they reach the application, protecting against unauthorized users at the edge. Handling fraud logic in Lambda or converting to a private API does not scale as a bot mitigation, and per-user IAM roles are impractical for public consumers.
160: C is correct because the dataset is tiny at only 300 MB per month, so Amazon S3 Standard stores it at negligible cost while providing immediate, millisecond access whenever the disaster recovery copy is needed, and the data can simply be deleted after 30 days. S3 Glacier has retrieval delays and retrieval fees that make it unnecessary for such a small dataset, and OpenSearch Service or RDS for PostgreSQL would add provisioning costs and operational overhead far exceeding the storage need.
